lesson.title: The Adjustable Resistor: Dialing In Voltage With a Twist
lesson.summary: A potentiometer adds a sliding third contact to a resistor, letting you split one fixed total resistance into two variable pieces by turning a knob.
lesson.body:
A fixed resistor gives you exactly one resistance value forever. A potentiometer is built from the same resistive material, but it adds a third contact, a sliding or rotating wiper that rides along the resistive track between the two end terminals. As you turn the knob or slide the lever, the wiper's position along the track changes, which changes how much resistance lies between the wiper and each end. The full resistive element still has one total value, printed on the case, but the potentiometer lets you split that total two different ways at will.

There are two common ways to wire a potentiometer. Used as a rheostat, only the wiper and one end terminal are connected into the circuit, so the device behaves like a single variable resistor whose value changes as you turn it, useful for things like adjusting current into an LED. Used as a voltage divider, all three terminals are connected: the two ends go to a voltage source and ground, and the wiper taps off a fraction of that voltage. Because the wiper splits the total resistance into two pieces in series, call them R1 from the top end to the wiper and R2 from the wiper to ground, the output voltage follows the same divider relationship as two fixed resistors: Vout equals Vin times R2 divided by the sum of R1 and R2.

Take a 10 kilohm potentiometer wired across a 9 volt supply, with the wiper turned to 30 percent of its rotation measured from the grounded end. That means 30 percent of the total resistance, 3000 ohms, lies between the wiper and ground, so R2 is 3 kilohms, and the remaining 7 kilohms is R1. Applying the divider formula: Vout equals 9 volts times 3 kilohms divided by 10 kilohms, which is 9 times 0.3, giving 2.7 volts at the wiper. Turn the knob further toward the top and R2 grows, raising Vout smoothly toward the full 9 volts.

Physically, potentiometers come with different tapers, meaning how resistance changes with rotation. A linear taper potentiometer splits resistance in direct proportion to the wiper's mechanical position, which is what the example above assumed. An audio or logarithmic taper changes resistance on a curve instead, because the human ear perceives loudness logarithmically, so volume knobs on amplifiers and radios almost always use log taper parts to make the loudness increase feel even as you turn the knob.

At its core, a potentiometer is nothing more exotic than the resistor you already know, reshaped into two resistors in series that share one moving junction. Everything you learned about how resistors set current and divide voltage still applies, the potentiometer just lets the split point move under your hand instead of being fixed at the factory. That simple trick is why potentiometers show up everywhere from volume knobs and dimmer switches to joystick position sensors and throttle pedals in cars.
